podcasts.title: Powering AI-Driven Drug Discovery with President of Isomorphic Labs Max Jaderberg
podcasts.description:
Drug discovery and development has long relied on expensive, time-consuming empirical trial and error. By shifting the discovery process onto computers, Isomorphic Labs wants to fundamentally change medicine from a process of discovery to one of precision engineering. Elad Gil sits down with Isomorphic’s president Max Jaderberg to discuss his vision for using predictive AI models to achieve experimental accuracy. Max details how the success of AlphaFold provided the first proof of concept that a deep learning model could generalize in the field of biology, and how an AI model’s compounding of learnings allows it to achieve generalizability with scale, thus greatly increasing the probability of success as well as speed in real world clinical trials. He also talks about evolving past the need for animal testing through in-silico models, Isomorphic’s focus on developing drug design engines that are agnostic of disease area, target class, and modality, why accurate molecule engineering unlocks the potential for multidrug cocktails that span complex biological pathways, and how he believes AI molecule optimization will improve both human lifespan and healthspan.

The heart of our conversation is what he sees as the central flaw in American healthcare, which is that the patient is not the customer. He points to GLP-1s and LASIK as examples of what’s possible when patients pay directly, and he thinks AI could bring healthcare down to the price of a Netflix subscription.

But to capture that opportunity, Zach first had to rebuild Ro's culture around high performance and a big heart. It shows in the stories Ro shares from people like Serena Williams, which help patients get past the stigma of seeking treatment. The inspiration behind it all is his father, a doctor whose care Zach wants to recreate in software.

podcasts.title: How To Build The Future: Paul Graham & Amjad Masad
podcasts.description: Replit was building toward the AI coding era years before it had a name. In 2024, the company shipped an agent that could take a request in plain English, work through errors, provision its own infrastructure, and keep going until the software actually worked. The model companies even reached out to ask how Replit had pulled it off.Co-founder and CEO Amjad Masad had been thinking about making programming radically more accessible since 2008, and Replit’s original pitch deck predicted AI-generated code before the Transformer paper was published. Today, that same technology is moving into banks, manufacturers, and other large companies, where Amjad says teams are replacing software projects once scoped at $10 million with $250,000 of Replit.On How to Build the Future, Paul Graham sits down with Amjad to talk about why Replit was so well positioned when coding agents arrived, what comes after vibe coding, and his bigger vision for the “self-driving company,” where AI agents increasingly build and operate the software a company needs.
